questions.question:
Read the passage about John Roebling and the Brooklyn Bridge, then answer:
(a) Who was John Roebling? What did he want to do?
(b) How did the building experts react to Roebling's idea?
(c) What was the result of the tragic accident?
(d) How did Washington communicate with his wife?
(e) What two places does the bridge connect?
(f) What is the name of the bridge?
(g) Find the words from the passage which mean the same as (i) beautiful (1st para) (ii) disability (4th para).
questions.answer:
### (1(a))

**Answer.** John Roebling was **a creative engineer**. He wanted to **build a spectacular bridge connecting New York with the Long Island**.

**What the passage says.**

> "In 1857, a creative engineer named John Roebling was inspired by an idea to build a spectacular bridge. The bridge would connect New York with the Long Island."

**What else we learn about him.** Bridge-building experts told him the idea was impossible and advised him to forget it, but "Roebling could not ignore the vision he had in his mind"; he persuaded his son Washington, also an engineer, that the bridge could be built, and father and son worked out the concepts and overcame the obstacles together.

**Model two-mark answer.** John Roebling was a creative engineer who, in 1857, conceived the idea of a spectacular bridge joining New York with the Long Island. He wanted to convert that vision into a real bridge, in the face of expert opinion that it was impossible, and he persuaded his son Washington to help him.

### (1(b))

**Answer.** The building experts reacted **negatively**. They said the idea was an "impossible task" and advised him to **forget it** — it "could not be done", it was not practical and it "had never been done before".

**The passage's words.**

> "All the bridge building experts throughout the world thought that this was an impossible task. They told Roebling to forget the idea. It could not be done. It was not practical. It had never been done before."

**Why they reacted so.** No bridge of that span had ever been built, the technology of the time seemed unequal to it, and the experts were unwilling to risk their reputations on an untried design. Their reaction also gives the story its theme: the vision of one man against the received wisdom of the world.

**Model two-mark answer.** The experts dismissed the plan outright. They called it an impossible, impractical task that had never been attempted, and they told Roebling to forget it altogether — a reaction that makes his later achievement a triumph of vision over expert opinion.

### (1(c))

**Answer.** The accident **killed John Roebling and caused brain damage to Washington Roebling**, leaving him unable to **walk, talk or even move**.

**The passage's words.**

> "The project started well, but when it was only a few months under way a tragic accident happened on the site. It killed John Roebling. Washington was injured and left with a partial brain damage. He would no longer be able to walk or talk or even move."

**What followed.** Because the Roeblings were the only people who knew how the bridge could be built, "everyone had a negative comment to make" and felt the project should be scrapped. Washington, however, was not discouraged: though bedridden, he still had "a burning desire to complete the bridge".

**Model two-mark answer.** The accident on the site killed John Roebling and left his son Washington with partial brain damage, so that he could no longer walk, talk or even move. Everyone concluded that the project should be abandoned, since the only two men who knew how to build the bridge were dead or helpless.

### (1(d))

**Answer.** Washington communicated with his wife **by a code of communication using the help of a single finger**. He touched her arm with his finger to tell her what to tell the engineers.

**The passage's words.**

> "All he could do was move one finger and he decided to make the best use of it. By moving this, he slowly developed a code of communication with his wife. He touched his wife's arm with his finger and told her to tell the engineers what to do."

**How long it went on.** For **thirteen years** Washington "tapped out his instructions with his finger on his wife's arm", until the bridge was completed in 1883. She "patiently decoded the message of her husband and told the engineers what to do."

**Model two-mark answer.** Paralyzed except for one finger, Washington developed a code and tapped out his instructions on his wife's arm. She decoded them and passed them on to the engineers, and in this way the two of them directed the construction for thirteen years, until the bridge opened in 1883.

### (1(e))

**Answer.** The bridge connects **New York with the Long Island**.

**The passage's words.**

> "The bridge would connect New York with the Long Island."
> "The bridge connects New York and Long Island."

**Background detail worth one line.** This is the Brooklyn Bridge, completed in 1883, which spans the East River between Manhattan (New York City) and Brooklyn on Long Island — "the spectacular Brooklyn Bridge", as the passage calls it at the close.

**Model two-mark answer.** The Brooklyn Bridge connects New York with the Long Island, spanning the river between them. It was the fulfilment of John Roebling's vision, begun in 1857 and completed in 1883, twenty-six years later.

### (1(f))

**Answer.** **The Brooklyn Bridge.**

**The passage's words.**

> "Today the spectacular Brooklyn Bridge stands in all its glory."

**One-mark answer.** The bridge is the Brooklyn Bridge (completed in 1883).

**Note on why the name is worth remembering.** The passage never names it at the beginning — it speaks only of "a spectacular bridge" to connect New York with the Long Island — and reveals the name only in the closing paragraph, so the question tests whether the whole passage has been read.

### (1(g))

**Answers.**

| Word | Word from the passage |
|---|---|
| (i) **beautiful** | **spectacular** |
| (ii) **disability** | **handicap** |

**Where they occur.**

- Para 1: "a creative engineer named John Roebling was inspired by an idea to build a **spectacular** bridge" — *spectacular* means striking, magnificent, beautiful.
- Para 4: "In spite of his **handicap** Washington was never discouraged" — the *handicap* is the partial brain damage that left him unable to walk, talk or move.

**Note on the printed key.** The booklet gives "(i) spectacular (ii) handicap", agreeing with the analysis above.

**Marking tip.** After the word, add a two-word gloss to show you understand it ("spectacular = striking/magnificent"), which secures the mark even if the examiner doubts the match.

questions.question:
Read the passage on the Himalayas, then answer:
(a) Make notes on the passage in points only, using headings, sub-headings and abbreviations; also suggest a suitable title.
(b) Write a summary of the passage in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
### (a) Notes and title

**Title: The Himalayas**

**1. The Himalayas — the range**
   1.1 Series of mountain ranges, arc of 2,500 km, Pakistan to Tibet
   1.2 Largest mountain system in the world
   1.3 30 mountains over 7,300 m above sea level
   1.4 Jagged snow-capped peaks, large valley glaciers
   1.5 19 large rivers drain it — Indus, Brahmaputra
   1.6 Rivers carry mud/silt → fertile plains of India & Bangladesh
   1.7 Crops: rice, cotton

**2. Formation**
   2.1 About 38 million years ago
   2.2 Indian plate collided with Eurasian plate
   2.3 Still rising today

**3. Climate**
   3.1 Different on north and south sides
   3.2 South: India & Pakistan protected from cold northern air; temperate
   3.3 North: no moisture, very dry; Tibet = desert conditions

**4. Crops, animals, produce**
   4.1 Rice, cereals, sugarcane in river valleys & hill terraces
   4.2 Fruit orchards, vineyards, tea plantations on lower slopes
   4.3 Sheep, goats, yaks; yaks carry people & loads
   4.4 One-third forested → paper, matches, other products, firewood

**5. Other resources**
   5.1 Valuable minerals & gemstones
   5.2 Iron ore, coal
   5.3 Rivers dammed for hydroelectric power

**6. Problems**
   6.1 High mountains → roads, railways difficult
   6.2 Many communities isolated

**Marking scheme reminder.** Notes must be **points only**, with abbreviations (km, m, &) and consistent numbering; the **title** carries a mark of its own. Copying whole sentences from the passage loses marks — the examiner wants keywords.

### (b) Summary

**Summary (about 80 words).**

The Himalayas form the world's largest mountain system, a 2,500-km arc from Pakistan to Tibet, with thirty peaks above 7,300 m. They began rising about 38 million years ago when the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate and are still rising. They give India a temperate climate and Tibet a desert one, and their rivers carry fertile silt to the plains. Their valleys grow rice, cereals and sugarcane, their slopes orchards and tea, and their forests and minerals support the people.

**Why this summary works.**

- It covers all six blocks of the passage: **scale, formation, climate, agriculture, resources, isolation**.
- It keeps the **numerical facts** that give the passage its substance (2,500 km, 7,300 m, 38 million years) but drops the examples that cannot fit an 80-word limit.
- It is continuous prose, in the **third person and present tense** — a summary is not a set of notes.
- It stays within the word limit; going beyond 80 words earns no extra marks.

questions.question: You are Supriya/Ravi, Class President of Class XII of J. P. Inter College, Dhanbad. You are collecting old clothes for the beggars of your town. Write a notice for the students of Class XI and XII, inviting them to participate in the collection. (50 words)
questions.answer:
**J. P. INTER COLLEGE, DHANBAD**

**NOTICE**

**1 March 2014**

**COLLECTION OF OLD CLOTHES FOR THE BEGGARS**

All the students of Class XI and XII are hereby informed that we are collecting old clothes for the poor beggars of our town. All of you are invited to contribute to the collection. Please submit some old clothes to the Class President before 12 March 2014.

**Supriya**
Class President, XII

**Format checklist.**

1. Institution's name, the word **NOTICE**, and the **date**.
2. A **caption** announcing the purpose.
3. **Body** naming the beneficiaries (beggars of the town), the action required (contribute old clothes), and the **deadline** (12 March 2014).
4. **Signature with designation** at the bottom left.
5. **50 words**, in a box — a notice is meant to be read at a glance.

**Why the deadline and the addressee matter.** Without "before 12 March" and "to the Class President" the notice gives no actionable instruction, and marks are cut even if every other element is present.

questions.question: You are Anamika/Aniket and your birthday is on the 2nd of March. Write an invitation for your friends asking them to come to a party at 5:00 p.m. (50 words)
questions.answer:
**M.G. Road, Ranchi**
**1 March 2014**

**Dear Friends**

It gives me great pleasure to invite you to my house for my birthday celebration party on **2 March 2014**. I am sure you will enjoy a great party, and we will have great fun together. The party will start at **5:00 p.m. onwards**. Do come — your presence will make the day complete.

**Yours sincerely**
**Aniket**

**Format checklist for an informal invitation.**

1. Sender's **address** and **date** (an informal invitation carries these, unlike a printed card).
2. Word of **salutation** ("Dear Friends") — informal invitations to friends use this, not "Respected Sir".
3. **Occasion, date and time** clearly stated: birthday, 2 March 2014, 5:00 p.m.
4. **Venue**: "my house" (which is exactly what the question permits).
5. Complimentary close "Yours sincerely" and the **name**.
6. **50 words**, in the ordinary letter form — not in a boxed notice.

**Note on the printed model.** The booklet's answer opens "M.G. Road / Ranchi / 1st March, 2014" and closes "Yours Sincerely / Aniket"; the version above keeps that shape and adds the missing date and time in the body.

questions.question: You did not go home for Holi. You stayed back in the hostel/lodge because you had to study for the exams. Describe how much you missed Holi with your family members. (125 words)
questions.answer:
**HOLI AWAY FROM HOME**

Holi is the most colourful and enjoyable festival of India. We observe it with great zest and fanfare. This year, however, I stayed back at the hostel, because my examinations were only a fortnight away, and I did not go home.

The hostel did celebrate. The students embraced one another and smeared each other's faces with coloured powder called "gulal"; the more adventurous added fast colours in buckets of water and threw them on everyone. With faces smeared with colour we all looked like ghosts, sweets and tea were exchanged, and dancing and singing lifted the spirits of even the gloomiest soul. Yet the celebrations at the hostel still haunt my memory as a poor copy of home.

I missed my family terribly. My father, mother, brother and sisters were waiting for me, and I could not be with them. A festival is nothing without the people it is meant to be shared with; the colours were there, but the home was missing.

**What makes this answer score.**

- It answers the question asked: **how much** Holi was missed, not merely what Holi is.
- It has a clear **structure**: what Holi means → what happened in the hostel → what was missing.
- It uses **sensory detail** (gulal, buckets of water, ghost-like faces, sweets and tea) and one **reflective sentence** at the close.
- It is written in the **first person and past tense** — this is a personal description, unlike a report.
- It stays within 125 words.

questions.question: You are Tusu/Sunaram of C. P. Republic College, Ranchi. The students of your college participated in a 'Run for Peace' organised by NSS. Prepare a report about the event to be published in the school magazine. (125 words)
questions.answer:
**RUN FOR PEACE**

**C. P. Republic College, Ranchi**
**By Tusu**

**28 February 2014.** Everybody in the world wants to live in peace. For this great social issue, the N.S.S. organised a "Run for Peace" in which a large number of people took part. Celebrities, M.L.A.s and government officers were also present. The run started at 8:00 a.m. and was completed at 9:30 a.m. The Chief Minister was the chief guest. The run was organised for 6 km, from the Army ground to the J.A.P. ground. Balloons, flowers and T-shirts bearing the message of peace made the participants look alike, and the uniformity of dress gave the morning a festive seriousness. It was a great show of unity for peace, and the organisers have resolved to make it an annual event.

**Format checklist for a magazine report.**

1. **Headline** in capitals, then the **institution** and **by-line**.
2. **Date line** and the opening statement of purpose.
3. **Facts in sequence**: organiser, participation, dignitaries, timings, route and distance.
4. **Closing sentence** on the significance of the event.
5. **Third person and past tense**; no "I" or personal opinion beyond the closing remark.
6. **125 words**, and a formal, neutral register suitable for a school magazine.

**Why the details matter.** A report earns marks for **verifiable particulars** — 6 km, 8:00 to 9:30 a.m., Army ground to J.A.P. ground, the Chief Minister as chief guest — not for adjectives.

questions.question: You are Noel/Nelly, Head Boy/Girl of K. B. Memorial High School, Bokaro. Write an application to the Principal asking for permission to organise a class picnic. (125 words)
questions.answer:
**Noel**
Head Boy, Class XII-A
K. B. Memorial High School, Bokaro

**1 March 2014**

**To
The Principal
K. B. Memorial High School
Bokaro**

**Sub: Application for permission to organise a class picnic**

**Sir**

Respectfully, I wish to submit that our school has been organising class picnics for the batches of Class XII every year.

In respect of this, and in view of the desire of the students, I request you to allow us to organise a class picnic for Class XII this session. We propose to go to a nearby picnic spot on a Saturday, travelling by the school bus, and to return before dusk. Two teachers will accompany us, and we shall take every care of discipline and safety. The expenses will be met by the students themselves.

We shall be ever grateful to you for your kind permission.

**Yours obediently**
**Noel**
Head Boy, Roll No. 35, Class XII-A

**Format checklist.**

1. Sender's **name, designation and class** at the top, then the **date**, then the Principal's address.
2. **Subject line** stating the request precisely.
3. Body: the precedent (picnics held earlier), the **specific proposal** (place, day, transport, escort, expenses), and the **assurance** of discipline.
4. Close "Yours obediently" with name and designation.
5. Courteous, respectful tone throughout; **125 words**.

**Why the specifics earn marks.** A Principal sanctions a trip only if the plan is concrete — who escorts the students, how they travel, when they return, and who pays.

questions.question: During elections many political parties paint slogans on the walls of houses which look very ugly. Write a letter to the Editor of 'The Telegraph' expressing your concern. (125 words)
questions.answer:
**M.G. Road, Ranchi**
**1 March 2014**

**To
The Editor
The Telegraph
Kolkata**

**Sub: Defacement of walls by election slogans**

**Sir**

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper I wish to express my concern at the way political parties deface the walls of houses and public buildings with slogans during elections.

Every election season the town is plastered with paint. House-owners who object are ignored or intimidated, and the walls of schools, hospitals and even heritage buildings are not spared. The result is an ugliness that no amount of whitewash can remove, and an expense that falls on the citizen, not on the party. Election publicity can perfectly well be carried on through posters at designated sites and through the media.

I request the authorities to enforce the rules against defacement strictly, and I hope your paper will take up the matter.

**Yours faithfully**
**Noel**

**Format checklist for a letter to the editor.**

1. Sender's address and **date**, then "The Editor" and the paper's address.
2. **Subject line**.
3. Salutation "Sir/Madam"; body stating the **problem**, giving **evidence and consequences**, and proposing a **remedy**.
4. Close "Yours faithfully" with the writer's name.
5. Formal, restrained tone — a letter to the editor argues, it does not abuse.
6. **125 words**.
